unit.title: Prepare and install cable trays - basic

summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to plan and lead a cable tray installation. You will choose the tray type and material, work out supports, loads and fill from the maker's data, plan safe work at height, fix and join the tray, bond it to earth and test it. You will also lead the laying of cables, keep systems apart, and inspect and hand over the job with its records.

blocks.p: A cable tray is an open support for cables. It does not enclose them as conduit or trunking does: it carries them, lets air cool them and lets cables be added later. Trays carry the main cable routes of factories, hotels, hospitals, plant rooms and data rooms. At Level 3 you plan the tray job, do the calculations, lead the team and sign the records.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Read the drawings and specification
Find the tray type, width, finish, height, spare capacity, support method and bonding requirement. Raise a written query on anything unclear or in conflict.
Survey the route
Walk the route with the other trades' drawings. Find clashes with beams, ducts, pipes and sprinklers before anything is ordered.
Choose tray, fittings and materials
Match the tray type to the cables and the material and finish to the conditions.
Do the calculations
Work out the number of lengths, splices and supports, the load on the tray and on each support, and the tray fill.
Plan safe work
Choose the access, set exclusion zones, plan lifting, isolate nearby circuits and write the method statement and risk assessment.
Set out and fix supports
Mark a straight, level line; fix brackets and hangers at the planned span with anchors chosen from the maker's data.
Cut, join and bond the tray
Cut and treat the tray, assemble splices to the maker's torque, allow for expansion, bond the tray and test continuity.
Lead the cable laying
Plan the pull, protect the cable's bending radius, space and fix the cables, and keep power, control and data apart.
Inspect, snag and hand over
Inspect against the drawing, correct faults, and hand over as-built drawings, test records and the maker's data.
Supervise others
Brief the team, check early work, correct mistakes by showing the right method, and keep the records.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Span
The distance between the centres of two supports.
Safe working load (SWL)
The most load the tray may carry at a given span, from the maker's table, usually in kilograms per metre (kg/m).
Splice (splice plate)
The bolted plate that joins two lengths of tray.
Trapeze hanger
Two threaded rods from the ceiling with a strut across them, on which the tray sits.
Bonding jumper
A short conductor fixed across a joint so that the earth path is continuous.
Earth, earthing (British) / ground, grounding (NEC)
The same thing. Jamaica's code is based on the US NEC, so you will hear both sets of words.
Protective conductor (British) / equipment grounding conductor (NEC)
The conductor that connects metal parts back to the earth bar.

blocks.note: Jamaican conditions are hard on tray systems: strong sun, salt air along the coasts, heavy rain and hurricane winds. They decide the material, the fixings, the cable ties and how covers are held down. JPS supplies 110 V and 220 V at 50 Hz, and a new or altered installation is inspected by a licensed electrical inspector, under the Government Electrical Regulator, before it is connected.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Read the sections in order: they follow the job. Work every example with a calculator. Load tables in this kit are examples for practice: on a real job the figures come from the maker of the tray you are fitting. Then try the practice test and read each explanation.

head: Type
Description
Strengths
Limits
Typical use
rows: Ladder tray
Two side rails joined by rungs
Strongest over long spans; free air round the cables; cables can drop out between rungs
Gives no support between rungs, so it does not suit small, soft cables
Large, heavy power cables in factories and plant rooms
Perforated tray
A flat base with slots or holes, and upturned sides
Supports cables along their length; some air flow; ties go through the slots
Shorter spans and lighter loads than ladder tray
Mixed small and medium power and control cables
Wire mesh (basket) tray
A welded wire grid
Light; quickly cut and shaped on site; easy to add and change cables
Light loads and short spans
Data and small cables in offices, data rooms and above ceilings
Solid-bottom tray with cover
A closed base and a lid
Shields cables from dust, sun, falling objects and interference
Holds heat in, so power cables may need derating; water can collect
Dusty or exposed places; sensitive signal cables

head: Material
Where it suits
Watch out for
rows: Pre-galvanised steel (zinc coated before forming)
Dry indoor places
Thin coating; cut and punched edges have none.
Hot-dip galvanised steel (dipped after making)
Damp, outdoor and industrial places
Thick coating, but every cut made on site must be treated with zinc-rich paint.
Stainless steel
Sea-front sites, food and chemical plants
Cost; use stainless fixings.
Aluminium
Outdoor runs where low weight matters
Corrodes where it touches steel in damp air, so use the maker's isolating washers or matching fixings. It also expands about twice as much as steel.
Fibreglass (GRP)
Very corrosive places and the coast
Does not conduct, so it cannot be bonded; lower strength when hot; needs the UV-resistant grade outdoors.

blocks.p: When two different metals touch in damp or salty air, one of them corrodes much faster. This is **galvanic corrosion**. It is why aluminium tray is not bolted straight onto steel brackets, and why bolts, washers and clamps come from the tray maker's own range.

head: Fitting
Use
rows: Horizontal bend
Turns the run left or right in the same level, usually at 90° or 45°.
Vertical riser bends (inside and outside)
Take the run up or down. A pair lifts the tray over a duct or beam and brings it back to level.
Tee and cross
A tee joins three runs; a cross joins four runs at one point.
Reducer
Joins a wide tray to a narrower one.
Splice plates
Join lengths end to end. Expansion splices let the lengths slide.
Divider (barrier strip)
A metal strip along the tray that keeps one group of cables apart from another.
Cover
Protects cables from sun, dust and falling objects.
Drop-out
A curved fitting where cables leave the tray downwards, so they bend gently and do not bear on an edge.
Cable cleats and clamps
Hold large cables firmly, especially on vertical runs.

blocks.p: On a planned job, bends, tees and risers are **factory-made**. They keep the strength the maker tested and a bend radius that suits the cables, and they splice like any straight length. A bend cut and folded from straight tray on site is weaker, has raw edges and may be too tight for the cables. Wire mesh tray is the exception: it is designed to be cut and formed on site, following the maker's cutting pattern and using the maker's bolts at each cut.

ul: Find the tray type, width, depth, material and finish; the fixing height; the support method and spacing; the fill limit; and the bonding and test requirements.

**Spare capacity** is space left free for future cables. '25% spare' means the cables fitted today use no more than three-quarters of the space, and the tray's load must allow for the extra cables too. It never means the tray may be loaded beyond the maker's rating.
Check the revision of every drawing. If two drawings disagree, for example on the tray height, do not choose one and do not split the difference: **raise a query and get the answer in writing**.

blocks.p: Tray shares the ceiling space with ducts, pipes, sprinkler mains and structural beams. Walk the route with the other trades' drawings in your hand. A clash found on paper costs a telephone call; a clash found after the tray is up costs a day's work. Agree the route and levels at a coordination meeting, and have the change recorded. Tray is never hung from another trade's pipes, ducts or ceiling grid, and other trades do not hang their work from the tray.

From the drawings, list every item with its quantity: tray lengths, bends, tees, risers and reducers; splice plates and bolts; brackets, strut, threaded rod, nuts, washers and anchors; bonding jumpers, the earth conductor and lugs; covers, dividers and drop-outs; zinc-rich paint; cable ties, cleats and labels. Check the **cable schedule** against the tray: is the width enough, is the fill within the limit, and is the weight within the load?

head: Plan
Points to settle
rows: Access
Work platform, mobile tower or podium; who is trained to use it; floor condition.
Lifting
How lengths of tray, and later the cable, get to height.
People below
Work times agreed with the occupier; exclusion zones; signs.
Existing services
Scanning before drilling; which circuits must be isolated, and when.
Order of work
Supports, tray, bonding and test, cables, fire stopping, inspection.
Storage
Tray stacked flat and dry on site, off the ground, where it will not be walked on.
Records
Who records the tests, the as-built route and the photographs of hidden work.
Rescue
How a person stuck or hurt at height will be brought down.

flow: Read documents; raise queries
Survey with other trades; agree route and levels
Calculations and take-off; order materials
Method statement, risk assessment, team briefing
Set out the line; scan; fix supports
Fit and splice the tray; bond it
Test continuity and record
Lay, space and fix the cables
Fire stopping; labels
Inspect, snag, as-built drawings and handover

sections.title: Calculations: lengths, supports, loads and fill

ul: Number of lengths = run ÷ length of one piece, **rounded up**. A 34 m run in 3 m lengths: 34 ÷ 3 = 11.3, so 12 lengths.
A straight run of whole lengths has one fewer splice joint than lengths: 12 lengths have 11 joints. Each joint needs a pair of splice plates, one on each side rail.
Add the fittings: every bend, tee or riser adds its own joints.

blocks.p: For a straight run with a support at each end: number of spans = run ÷ span, **rounded up**; number of supports = spans + 1. Rounding up makes each span a little shorter than the limit, never longer.

blocks.note: **Example.** A 34 m run with a span limit of 2.5 m: 34 ÷ 2.5 = 13.6, so 14 spans, and 14 + 1 = **15 supports**. The actual spacing is 34 ÷ 14 = 2.43 m. Thirteen spans would be 2.62 m each: over the limit.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The maker's table gives the safe working load for each tray at each span. **The longer the span, the lower the load.** Add up the weight per metre of every cable from the cable data, and compare it with the table. Allow for the future cables that the spare capacity is meant for.

head: Span (example table for one tray)
Safe working load
rows: 60 kg/m
40 kg/m
28 kg/m
20 kg/m

blocks.p: **Example.** The cables weigh 17 kg/m and the specification asks for 25% spare capacity. Allow for 17 × 1.25 = 21.25 kg/m. At a 3.0 m span the tray is rated 20 kg/m: not enough. At 2.5 m it is rated 28 kg/m: enough, with a margin. At 2.0 m it is also enough, but needs more supports than the job requires. Choose **2.5 m**, record the working, and check that it suits the structure.

Each support in the middle of a run carries half of the span on each side of it: one full span of loaded tray. Load on a support = (cable weight + tray weight per metre) × span. The brackets, rods and anchors must each be rated for that load, with the margin the maker's data gives.

blocks.note: **Example.** Cables 17 kg/m, tray 5 kg/m, span 2.5 m. Each intermediate support carries (17 + 5) × 2.5 = **55 kg**. On a trapeze hanger with two rods, each rod and its anchor takes about half of that, when the load is central.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Usable area of the tray = inside width × usable depth.
Area of one cable = 3.14 × d × d ÷ 4, where d is its overall diameter.
Fill = total cable area ÷ usable area × 100. Compare it with the limit in the specification.
Example: a tray 450 mm × 50 mm has 22,500 mm². Cables adding up to 7,200 mm² fill 7,200 ÷ 22,500 × 100 = 32%. With a 40% limit this passes.
If the fill is over the limit, use a wider or deeper tray or a second run. Do not pile the cables higher than the sides.

blocks.h: Width for cables laid in one layer

blocks.p: Large power cables are laid in a single layer, often with a gap between them, so that they can lose heat. The width needed is the sum of the cable diameters plus the gaps, plus the spare space. Example: five cables of 30 mm laid touching need 150 mm; with a gap of one cable diameter between them they need 5 × 30 + 4 × 30 = 270 mm, so a 300 mm tray is the smallest standard size before any spare space is added.

blocks.note: A tray is not a walkway or a step. Its load table allows for cables, not for a person's weight on one spot. Standing on a tray can bend it, loosen its splices and damage the cables, and the damage may not show until later.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Working safely on a tray job

blocks.p: Most tray is fixed overhead, so falls and falling objects are the main dangers. Start by asking what can be done on the ground: trapeze hangers can be assembled and tray lengths spliced in pairs before they are lifted.

head: Access
When it suits
Conditions
rows: Mobile elevating work platform (MEWP): scissor lift or boom
High work over a firm, level floor; long runs
Trained operators only; daily checks; a harness in boom types; nobody under the platform.
Mobile tower
Medium heights; work in one place for a while
Built by a competent person with guard rails and toe boards; wheels locked; never moved with people or loose tools on it.
Podium steps
Low-level work
Wheels locked; gate closed.
Ladder
Short, light tasks only
Not a working platform for fixing tray. Never tied to the tray or its brackets.

ul: Check access equipment before each use, and check that its inspection tag is in date.
Set an **exclusion zone** under the work with barriers and signs, and agree work times with the occupier.
**Tether hand tools** and keep fixings in a pouch or tray. A spanner dropped from 5 m can kill.
Never use a forklift and pallet, or a stack of anything, as a platform.
Have a rescue plan before anyone goes up.

blocks.p: A 3 m length of wide steel ladder tray is heavy and awkward, and wind catches it outdoors. Plan each lift: a hoist or the platform itself carries the tray up, with enough people to control it. Nobody climbs a ladder carrying tray, and tray is never rested on a guard rail to be slid into place.

ul: Check the drawings and **scan the slab or wall with a cable and pipe detector** before drilling for anchors.
Where a hanger must go beside an existing conduit or cable, that circuit is **isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead** first, with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after.
If a circuit cannot be switched off, move the support or change the route, or stop and refer it to the supervisor. Nobody works live.
In a ceiling space, do not load the ceiling grid or tiles, and fence off the area below.

head: Tool
PPE and precautions
rows: Hacksaw
Safety glasses and gloves; clamp the tray; support the off-cut.
Abrasive cut-off saw or grinder
Eye and face protection, ear protection and gloves; guards in place; sparks kept away from people and anything that burns; the site's hot-work rules.
Bolt cutters (wire mesh tray)
Safety glasses: cut wire ends fly. Cut to the maker's pattern so no sharp stubs are left.

blocks.p: Collect off-cuts and filings at once. They are sharp, they fall on people below, and filings left on a galvanised tray rust and stain it.

head: Support
Best where
Points
rows: Cantilever wall bracket
The tray runs along a strong wall or column
The bracket's rated load falls as the arm gets longer; fix with the anchors the maker's data gives.
Trapeze hanger: two threaded rods and a strut
The tray crosses open space below a slab or roof
Rods anchored into the structure; the strut set level; **lock nuts or double nuts** under the strut so it cannot creep down with vibration.
Centre hanger or clip
Light wire mesh tray
Light loads only, as the maker allows.
Floor stand or post
Rooftops and plant areas with nothing above
Bases fixed or weighted against wind; roof waterproofing protected.
Beam clamp
Steel beams and purlins
No drilling of structural steel without the engineer's approval.

ul: An anchor's size, type and depth are chosen from **the load it must carry and the maker's anchor data** for that base material, not from the drill bit that happens to be in the box.

Drill to the stated diameter and depth, clean the dust out of the hole, and set or tighten the anchor as the maker says. An anchor in a dusty or oversize hole can pull out under a fraction of its rating.
Each nut must have full thread through it. A nut that has caught only a few threads is a fault to record and put right.
Set a straight, level line with a laser level or chalk line, from the height on the drawing, and mark every support position on it before fixing any.
Fix the first and last supports, check them, then fill in between from the line. Supports set by eye from the last one drift.
Put supports near bends, tees and risers, as the maker's instructions show, because fittings carry extra load.

blocks.p: A splice is weaker than the unbroken tray. In the middle of a span, where the bending is greatest, a splice can sag or open. Plan the lengths so that each splice falls **near a support**, as the maker says; many makers ask for it within about a quarter of the span from a support. Splice bolts are tightened to the maker's **torque** with a torque wrench: a loose splice can move, and the earth path through it can fail.

Metal grows as it heats and shrinks as it cools. Typical figures are about 0.012 mm per metre for each 1 °C for steel and about 0.023 mm for aluminium. A tray on a roof in full sun can be tens of degrees hotter at midday than at night.

blocks.note: **Example.** A 50 m steel run changes temperature by 40 °C. Change in length = 50 × 40 × 0.012 = **24 mm**. An aluminium run would change by 50 × 40 × 0.023 = 46 mm. If the tray cannot move, it buckles, pulls its supports loose or breaks its splices.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Fit **expansion splices** at the spacing the maker gives for that material and temperature range, with the gap the maker's chart gives for the temperature on the day.
Fit one where the tray crosses a **building expansion joint**, because the two parts of the building move separately.
Near an expansion splice, hold the tray with **guide clamps** that let it slide, not hold-down clamps that grip it.
Leave slack in the cables at the joint.
An expansion splice slides, so it is not a reliable earth path: fit a **flexible bonding jumper** across it.

blocks.p: On a riser, the cables' whole weight tries to slide down. Fix them with cleats or ties at close, regular spacing, as the cable data and specification say, so that the weight is shared along the run and does not hang on the top fixing or on the terminations.

sections.title: Cutting, joining and bonding the tray

flow: Measure and mark the cut square
Clamp the tray and cut
Deburr and file every edge smooth
Treat cut galvanised edges with zinc-rich paint, as the maker says
Clear the filings before the piece goes up

blocks.p: Cutting removes the zinc from the edge. Zinc-rich paint (cold galvanising) puts protection back. Tape, oil or a quick pass with a torch does not.

ul: Use the maker's splice plates and bolts, with the bolt heads on the inside of the tray and the nuts outside, so no thread points at the cables.
Line up the lengths before tightening; then torque every bolt.
Fit factory bends, tees and risers with their own splices, and support them as the instructions show.
A pair of riser bends, one up and one down on each side, lifts the tray over an obstruction. Check that the largest cable can follow the bends without going below its minimum bending radius.

blocks.p: If a cable's insulation fails where it touches a metal tray, the tray becomes live. Bonded to earth, the tray carries the fault current back to the source, the protective device opens, and the danger is over in a fraction of a second. Unbonded, the whole run could stay live until someone touches it.

ul: The specification says how the tray is used. Often each circuit has **its own protective (earth) conductor**, and the tray is bonded as well. 'Not to be used as a circuit protective conductor, but bonded' means exactly that: the tray is earthed for safety, but it is not the earth wire for the circuits.

A bolted splice on clean metal, at the right torque, normally carries the bond. Fit a **bonding jumper** across any joint that cannot be relied on: an expansion splice, a painted or coated joint, a hinged or adjustable fitting, a gap in the run or a change of material.
Where a jumper is fixed, clean off paint and dirt so there is bare metal-to-metal contact.
Connect the tray to the main earthing terminal or the board's earth bar with a conductor of the size the specification gives.
A tray that carries only data cables is still metal near power circuits and equipment racks, so it is bonded as the specification says.

flow: Circuits on the tray isolated, or not yet connected
Check the low-resistance ohmmeter and its calibration date
Null the test leads
Measure from the earthing point to the far end and to the end of each branch
A reading much higher than the rest: test joint by joint
Clean and tighten the bad joint, or fit a jumper; retest
Write the results on the test record

blocks.note: **Nulling the leads** takes the leads' own resistance out of the reading. If the leads are not nulled, subtract their resistance yourself: a reading of 0.35 Ω with leads that measure 0.30 Ω on their own means the tray reads 0.05 Ω.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The test record goes in the handover file, with the instrument's serial number, the date and the tester's name. By the sea, splices corrode over the years, so the handover documents should recommend regular inspection and a repeat of the continuity test at set intervals.

head: Check or set up
Why
rows: Cable schedule: size, length and route
The right cable goes on the right tray.
Cable data: weight per metre, minimum bending radius, greatest pulling tension
They set the rollers, the bends and the method.
Drum on a stand or jacks at the start of the run, with a person at the brake
The cable comes off smoothly and does not over-run when the pull stops.
Straight rollers along the run; **corner rollers at every bend**
Rollers cut friction and protect the sheath; corner rollers hold the cable to a safe radius.
A person at each bend and at the drum; one leader; agreed calls or radios
Anyone can stop the pull at once.
A steady pull, by hand or by a winch with a tension limit
Jerks and too much force stretch and damage the cable.

ul: Minimum bending radius = the multiple in the data sheet × the cable's overall diameter. A 40 mm cable with a figure of 8 × D needs a radius of at least 320 mm. The tray's bends and the corner rollers must allow it; if a factory bend is tighter than the cable needs, a larger-radius bend is ordered.
If the cable sticks, **stop** and find the cause. Pulling harder is how sheaths are torn.
When the cable is in position, lift it off the rollers onto the tray with several people lifting together along its length. Do not lever it off, or drag it over the tray edge.
Seal the cut ends until the cable is terminated, so that water cannot get in.
Inspect the sheath along the route. Damage is reported and assessed before the cable is used; it is never hidden under a tie or tape.
Large power cables are laid in a **single layer**, spaced as the cable data and design say, so that heat can escape and the cables keep their current rating.
Cables piled in layers, or under a cover, lose heat less easily. The designer may have to derate them, which means larger cables.
Small control and data cables may be bundled, within the fill limit.

blocks.p: Power cables make magnetic fields and electrical noise. Data and control cables carry small signals that the noise can corrupt. A fault in a power cable can also put a dangerous voltage onto smaller cables. So the groups are kept apart.

ul: Best: **separate trays**, for example power on the upper tray and data on a lower one.
Or one tray with a fixed **metal divider**, with each group kept to its own side for the whole route.
Keep the separation distance the specification gives where trays run side by side.
Where power and data must cross, cross **at right angles**, so they run close together for the shortest possible length.
Cables of different voltages may share a section only if all are insulated for the highest voltage present.
Label trays and sections so that later workers keep the groups apart.

head: Place
Fixing
rows: Indoors, horizontal runs
Cable ties at even spacing, firm but not cutting into the sheath. Cut the tails flush with a tie tool: an angled cut leaves a sharp point that slices hands later.
Outdoors, in the sun
UV-resistant ties (usually black, and marked as such) or stainless steel ties. Ordinary ties go brittle and snap.
Vertical runs and large single cables
Cleats or clamps at the spacing the data gives.
Where cables leave the tray
A drop-out fitting or edge protection, so the cable bends gently and does not rest on a metal edge.
Data cable bundles
Wide, soft straps or loosely fitted ties; a crushed data cable loses performance.

blocks.p: A cover shades cables from the sun and keeps out dust and falling objects, but it holds heat in. Outdoors it must be held down with the maker's cover clamps at the stated spacing. A loose cover lifts in a strong wind, and in a hurricane it becomes a flying sheet of metal.

Where a tray passes through a fire-rated wall or floor, the opening is sealed round the cables with the approved fire-stop system. The tray itself usually stops each side of the wall, as the fire-stop maker's detail shows. Photograph the finished seal and record it **before** the ceiling is closed, because afterwards nobody can see whether it was done.

sections.title: Inspection, handover and supervising the team

head: Area
Check against the drawing and specification
rows: Tray
Right type, width, material and finish; right height and line; straight and level; no sharp edges; cut edges treated; no bent or damaged sections.
Supports
Position and span as calculated; supports near bends, tees and splices; anchors sound; nuts with full thread, and lock nuts fitted; rod ends not left where they can injure.
Joints
Splices near supports; bolts torqued; expansion splices and guide clamps where planned.
Bonding
Jumpers in place on clean metal; connection to earth; continuity results reviewed.
Cables
Fill within the limit; single layer and spacing where required; bending radius kept; ties and cleats correct; sheaths undamaged; labels at both ends.
Segregation
Each group on its own tray or side of the divider for the whole route; crossings at right angles.
Fire stopping
Done at every fire-rated wall and floor, with photographs.
Housekeeping
No off-cuts, filings, tools or tie tails left on the tray or the ceiling.

blocks.p: Every fault goes on a **snag list** with its location, what is wrong, who will correct it and by when. Faults are put right and then **rechecked** by someone other than the person who did the repair. Nothing is painted over, hidden by cables or left for the client to find. A fault that affects safety, such as a weak hanger, a missing bond or a cable on the wrong side of a divider, is cleared before the tray is put into use.

ul: **As-built drawings**: where the tray was actually installed, with every change of route or level.
The bonding continuity test record.
The signed inspection checklist and the closed-out snag list.
Photographs of hidden work, such as fire stopping and anchors above ceilings.
The maker's data and load tables, with your support and load calculation, so that the client knows how much more the tray may carry.
Any maintenance advice, such as inspecting splices and repeating the continuity test on coastal sites.

flow: Brief the team: drawing, method, hazards, roles
Show the standard: one support and one splice done correctly
Check each person's early work
Correct mistakes by showing the right method
Hold points: supports before tray, tray and bond before cables
Record checks and tests; review the job with the team

ul: When a trainee's work is wrong, stop the work, show how to set it out correctly, and have it corrected. Building the rest of the run to match a mistake, or leaving it for the cables to hide, makes the fault permanent.
If someone has done something unsafe, such as standing on the tray, deal with both parts: inspect for damage, and make sure the person and the team understand why it must not happen again.
Rotate the team leader's role on training jobs so that everyone learns to plan and check, not only to fix.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can compare ladder, perforated, wire mesh and solid covered tray and choose one for a given job.
I can choose a tray material and finish for indoor, outdoor and sea-front places, and explain galvanic corrosion.
I can name the common tray fittings and say why factory-made fittings are preferred.
I can explain what spare capacity means in a specification.
I can raise a query when drawings disagree, and survey a route for clashes with other trades.
I can prepare a take-off for a tray job.
I can work out the number of lengths, splice joints, spans and supports for a run.
I can check the cable load against the maker's load table and choose a span.
I can work out the load on one support.
I can work out the percentage fill of a tray and say what to do if it is too high.
I can choose access for work at height and set up exclusion zones and tool tethers.
I can plan the lifting of tray and the isolation of circuits near the work.
I can choose supports and explain how anchors are selected and set.
I can explain where splices should fall and why bolts are torqued.
I can work out how much a run will expand, and describe expansion splices, guide clamps and bonding jumpers.
I can cut tray and treat the cut edges.
I can explain why a tray is bonded, and what 'bonded but not used as a protective conductor' means.
I can test bonding continuity with nulled leads, find a bad joint and record the results.
I can plan and lead a heavy cable pull with rollers, signals and a controlled tension.
I can work out a cable's minimum bending radius and check the tray bends against it.
I can explain why cables are spaced and why power, control and data cables are kept apart.
I can choose cable ties and fixings for indoor, outdoor and vertical runs.
I can inspect a finished tray system, run a snag list and put together a handover pack.
I can brief, check and correct a team.

head: What
How
rows: Lengths of tray
Run ÷ length of one piece, rounded up
Splice joints in a straight run
Number of lengths − 1
Supports on a straight run
(Run ÷ span, rounded up) + 1
Cable load
Sum of the cables' kg/m; must not exceed the maker's safe working load at that span
Load on one support
(Cable kg/m + tray kg/m) × span
Fill
Total cable area ÷ (tray width × usable depth) × 100
Minimum bending radius
The data sheet's multiple × the cable's overall diameter
Expansion
Length (m) × temperature change (°C) × the figure for the material

terms: Anchor
A fixing set into concrete or masonry to carry a bracket or hanger rod.
As-built drawing
A drawing marked up to show where the tray was actually installed.
Bonding jumper
A short conductor fixed across a joint to keep the earth path continuous.
Cable roller
A free-turning roller set along the route so a cable can be pulled without dragging.
Cleat
A clamp that holds a large cable firmly to the tray.
Derating
Lowering the current a cable may carry because it cannot lose heat well.
Divider
A metal strip fitted along a tray to keep groups of cables apart.
Drop-out
A curved fitting that supports cables where they leave the tray downwards.
Exclusion zone
An area under or round the work that people are kept out of.
Expansion splice
A splice that lets two tray lengths slide as they heat and cool.
Fill
The share of the tray's usable cross-section taken up by cables.
Galvanic corrosion
Fast corrosion where two different metals touch in damp or salty air.
Guide clamp
A clamp that keeps the tray in line but lets it slide lengthways.
Hot-dip galvanising
Coating finished steel by dipping it in molten zinc.
MEWP
Mobile elevating work platform, such as a scissor lift.
Method statement
A written description of how a job will be done safely, step by step.
Nulling
Setting the ohmmeter so the resistance of its own leads is not counted.
Safe working load
The most load the tray may carry at a given span, usually in kg/m.
Snag list
A list of faults found at inspection, with who will correct each one.
Span
The distance between the centres of two supports.
Spare capacity
Space and load left free for cables to be added in future.
Splice
The bolted joint between two lengths of tray.
Trapeze hanger
Two threaded rods and a strut, hung from the structure to carry a tray.
Zinc-rich paint
Paint used to protect the cut edges of galvanised steel.

c1.title: A cold-store warehouse at Bernard Lodge
c1.text: Mr Clive Henry, a Level 3 electrician, is planning a straight 42 m run of ladder tray on trapeze hangers in a cold-store warehouse at Bernard Lodge, St Catherine. The cables on the schedule weigh 21 kg/m in total, and the specification asks for 25% spare capacity. For this tray the maker's table gives safe working loads of 45 kg/m at a 2.0 m span, 32 kg/m at 2.5 m and 24 kg/m at 3.0 m. On the coordination drawing, the tray would pass about 50 mm below the sprinkler main at one gridline, with a hanger position directly under the pipe.

c2.title: A server room at a university in Montego Bay
c2.text: Ms Nicole Edwards, a Level 3 electrician, leads the installation of wire mesh tray above the equipment racks in a new server room at a university in Montego Bay, St James. One tray will carry data cables and a second tray the 220 V feeds to the racks. The data tray has a usable cross-section of 300 mm × 90 mm, and the specification limits fill to 40%. Each data cable has an overall diameter of 6.2 mm, which gives an area of about 30.2 mm². At one point the power tray must pass over the data tray.

c3.title: An outdoor tray at a port near Rocky Point
c3.text: Mr Dwight Spencer, a Level 3 electrician, leads a team fitting a 60 m run of aluminium ladder tray with covers along an open pipe rack at an industrial port near Rocky Point, Clarendon, about 20 m from the sea. The tray is in full sun all day. The maker's data gives an expansion of 0.023 mm per metre for each 1 °C, and the tray's temperature can change by 35 °C between a cool night and a hot afternoon. The site is on an exposed stretch of the south coast.

c4.title: A heavy cable pull at a bottling plant in Twickenham Park
c4.text: Ms Keisha Morgan, a Level 3 electrician, leads six trainees pulling a four-core armoured cable along 55 m of ladder tray, 4 m above the floor of a bottling plant in Twickenham Park, St Catherine. The route has two horizontal 90° bends. The cable is 46 mm in overall diameter and weighs about 6.2 kg per metre, and its data sheet gives a minimum bending radius of 8 times the diameter. The factory bends already fitted to the tray have an inside radius of 300 mm.

c5.title: Final inspection above a mall corridor in Portmore
c5.text: Mr Ricardo Bailey, a Level 3 electrician, leads the final inspection of a 70 m perforated tray with a fixed divider above the service corridor of a shopping mall in Portmore, St Catherine. Power cables are meant to lie on one side of the divider and data cables on the other. During the inspection a trainee admits that he stood on the tray to reach a hanger. Ricardo also finds one 220 V cable lying on the data side for about 8 m, and a row of cable ties whose tails were cut at an angle with side cutters. The ohmmeter's leads were not nulled for the continuity test.

questions.q: Allowing for the 25% spare capacity, which span is the best choice for this run?
o: 3.0 m, because 24 kg/m is more than today's 21 kg/m
2.5 m, because 32 kg/m covers 21 kg/m plus a quarter
2.0 m, because the shortest span in a table is always best
3.0 m, because fewer hangers put less load on the roof
questions.why: Allow for the future cables: 21 × 1.25 = 26.25 kg/m. The 3.0 m span is rated only 24 kg/m, so it fails. The 2.5 m span (32 kg/m) passes with a margin. The 2.0 m span would pass too, but uses more hangers than the job needs.

questions.q: Clive settles on a span limit of 2.5 m, with a hanger at each end of the 42 m run. How many hangers does he need?
questions.why: 42 ÷ 2.5 = 16.8, so round up to 17 spans. Supports = spans + 1 = 18. The actual spacing is 42 ÷ 17 = 2.47 m, just inside the limit. Sixteen spans would be 2.63 m each: too long.

questions.q: What should Clive do about the tray passing 50 mm below the sprinkler main, with a hanger directly under the pipe?
o: Raise it with the other trades and agree a route in writing
Hang that length of tray from the sprinkler main with clips
Notch the side rail of the tray so that it clears the pipe
Fix the tray as drawn, and let the pipe fitter work round it
questions.why: A clash is settled before anything is ordered or fixed, by agreeing the route and levels with the other trades and recording the change. Tray is never hung from another trade's pipework, and cutting a side rail destroys the strength the load table depends on.

questions.q: About how many of the data cables may the data tray hold at the 40% fill limit?
o: About 281
About 536
About 357
About 894
questions.why: Usable area = 300 × 90 = 27,000 mm². At 40%: 0.4 × 27,000 = 10,800 mm². Number of cables = 10,800 ÷ 30.2 = 357.6, so 357 (round down). The figure of 894 is what would fill the tray completely, with no room to lay or add cables.

questions.q: How should the crossing be made where the power tray passes over the data tray?
o: At right angles, keeping the specified gap between them
With the two trays side by side for a few metres first
With the data cables lifted into the power tray to cross
At a shallow angle, so that neither tray needs a bend
questions.why: Interference grows with the length over which power and data cables run close together. Crossing at right angles keeps that length as short as it can be. The cables stay in their own trays, at the separation the specification gives.

questions.q: The data installer says the mesh tray carries only data cables, so it needs no connection to earth. What should Nicole reply?
o: That is right: only the trays with power cables are ever bonded
That is right, as long as plastic cable ties are used on it
It is bonded only if a data cable has a metal screen
It is still bonded, as the specification asks for metal tray
questions.why: The tray is metal, and it runs beside power feeds and equipment racks. A fault or a surge could make it live, and an unbonded tray can also add to interference. Metal tray is bonded and tested as the specification says, whatever it carries.

questions.q: Where bundles of data cable leave the mesh tray and drop to the racks, what should be fitted?
o: A tight cable tie that pulls each bundle against the tray's edge
A drop-out fitting that supports the cables round a gentle curve
A cover over that length of the tray to hold the bundles down
A divider strip fixed across the tray at the point of exit
questions.why: Cables hanging over a wire or a cut edge are bent too sharply and bear on a narrow point, which harms data performance and can cut the sheath in time. A drop-out (waterfall) fitting keeps the bend within the cable's minimum radius and spreads the load.

questions.q: By about how much could the length of the 60 m run change between the cool night and the hot afternoon?
o: About 5 mm
About 25 mm
About 48 mm
About 140 mm
questions.why: Change = length × temperature change × the maker's figure = 60 × 35 × 0.023 = 48.3 mm. That is far too much for fixed joints to take up, which is why the maker asks for expansion splices and guide clamps along a run like this.

questions.q: Why must the tray covers be fixed with the maker's cover clamps at the stated spacing, and not simply laid on?
o: Clamps are what make the covers shade the cables properly
Clamps stop the covers expanding when the sun is on them
Clamps keep rainwater from running along under the covers
Strong winds can lift loose covers and throw them about
questions.why: A cover is a light sheet with a large area. On an exposed coast, and above all in a hurricane, wind lifts loose covers, leaving the cables unprotected and sending sheet metal through the air. The maker's clamps and spacing are designed for wind loads.

questions.q: Given where this tray is, what should the handover documents recommend to the port's maintenance team?
o: Repainting the whole of the tray every year in a light colour
Regular inspection of joints, with continuity tests repeated
Removing the covers for good, so the splices can dry out
Tightening every splice bolt a little more each dry season
questions.why: Salt air attacks joints and fixings over the years, and a corroded splice can lose its earth path without looking very different. Regular inspection, with the bonding continuity test repeated and compared with the handover record, finds the problem before a fault does.

questions.q: What does the cable's data mean for the 300 mm factory bends already fitted?
o: They suit it, because the 8 × D figure applies only to conduit
They suit it, provided the cable is drawn round them slowly
They are too tight: this cable needs at least 368 mm
They are too tight: this cable needs at least 460 mm
questions.why: Minimum radius = 8 × 46 = 368 mm. The 300 mm bends would force the cable tighter than its maker allows, which can damage the insulation and armour however slowly it is pulled. Larger-radius bends must be fitted before the pull.

questions.q: Where must corner rollers be set up for this pull, and why?
o: At each bend, to hold the cable to a safe radius
At the drum only, to stop the cable running on after a stop
At the far end only, to lift the cable up to the pulling team
At every splice, to stop the cable catching on the bolt heads
questions.why: At a bend the pulling force drags the cable hard against the inside of the turn. Corner rollers carry it round at a controlled radius, so the sheath is not scraped on the side rail and the cable is not bent too tightly. Straight rollers do the same job along the straights.

questions.q: The cable is in position, lying on the rollers. How should it be moved onto the tray?
o: Pulled sideways over the rail by the people at the two ends
Levered off each roller in turn with a length of steel conduit
Left on the rollers, which are then tied down to the rungs
Lifted off by several people together, spaced along its length
questions.why: At 6.2 kg per metre, even a few metres of this cable is a heavy lift, so the team shares it along the length and lifts on one person's call. Levering or dragging it over the rail damages the sheath, and rollers are pulling equipment, not permanent supports.

questions.q: After the pull, Keisha finds the sheath scraped through to the armour for about 100 mm at one bend. What should she do?
o: Wrap the scrape in PVC tape and carry on with the next job
Turn the cable so that the scrape faces down onto the tray
Report it and have it assessed before the cable is used
Fit a cable tie over the scrape so that it cannot spread
questions.why: A damaged sheath lets moisture reach the armour, and the damage may go deeper than it looks. It is reported, recorded and assessed, and then repaired by the maker's approved method or the cable is replaced. Hiding it leaves a fault for someone else to find.

questions.q: What should Ricardo do about the trainee who stood on the tray?
o: Nothing, since the tray carried his weight without falling
Inspect that section for damage, and brief the team
Have that section's ties cut and replaced with new ones
Report him to the mall's manager and take him off the job
questions.why: A tray's load table allows for cables spread along it, not a person's weight on one spot. The section, its splices and hangers and the cables are checked for damage. The team is then told why it must not happen and given proper access, so the lesson is learned.

questions.q: What is the right way to deal with the 220 V cable lying on the data side of the divider?
o: Leave it there, as 8 m is too short a length to matter
Wrap that 8 m of the cable in foil tape to screen it off
Move the data cables over to the power side to match
Move it to the power side, and check the whole run
questions.why: Segregation works only if it holds for the whole route. A power cable among data cables causes interference, and a fault in it could put mains voltage on the data cabling. It is moved to its own side, the rest of the run is checked, and the item is closed on the snag list.

questions.q: The ohmmeter showed 0.35 Ω from the earth bar to the far end of the tray. Tested on their own, its leads measure 0.30 Ω. What is the tray's true reading?
questions.why: With the leads not nulled, the instrument measures the leads and the tray together: 0.35 − 0.30 = 0.05 Ω for the tray. Nulling the leads before the test does this subtraction for you. The corrected reading, and how it was found, go on the test record.

questions.q: Why should the cable ties with tails cut at an angle be put right before handover?
o: Angled tails let the ties work loose over a few months
Angled tails show that the wrong size of tie was used
The sharp points can cut the hands of later workers
The sharp points can pierce the sheath of the cable below
questions.why: A tie tail cut at an angle is a hard plastic blade at hand height for the next person who reaches into the tray. Tails are cut flush and square with a tie tool. It is a small defect, but one that injures people.

questions.q: The cables on a tray weigh 18 kg/m and the tray itself 6 kg/m. Trapeze hangers are 2 m apart. About what load does each hanger in the middle of the run carry?
o: 24 kg
48 kg
36 kg
96 kg
questions.why: Each middle hanger carries half a span from each side: one full span. Load = (18 + 6) × 2 = 48 kg. The strut, the two rods and their anchors must each be rated for their share of this, with the maker's margin.

questions.q: A hot-dip galvanised tray system is being chosen for a dry indoor plant room, and the client asks about using cheaper pre-galvanised tray instead. What is the main difference to explain?
o: Pre-galvanised tray has a thinner coating, bare at cut edges
Pre-galvanised tray cannot be bonded to the earthing system
Pre-galvanised tray is always weaker at the same span
Pre-galvanised tray may be used only with wire mesh fittings
questions.why: Pre-galvanised sheet is coated before it is cut and formed, so its coating is thin and its edges and holes are bare. That is acceptable in a dry indoor room. Hot-dip galvanising coats the finished tray thickly all over, which is what damp, outdoor and industrial places need.
